decks.title: Chemical Bonding — Part 1: The electrovalent bond
goals: Explain the formation of cations and anions by loss and gain of electrons
Define the electrovalent bond and draw orbit structures for sodium chloride, magnesium chloride and calcium oxide

slides.heading: Giving and taking
slides.body_md: Part 1 — atoms bond to reach a **stable outer shell**. In an **electrovalent bond** one atom gives electrons and another takes them.

visual.alt: Flow from a metal atom losing electrons and a non-metal atom gaining electrons to an ionic compound

slides.narration: Most atoms are not stable on their own. They bond to complete the outer shell. In this part, one kind of atom gives away electrons and another takes them, and the ions formed attract each other.

slides.heading: Why atoms bond
slides.body_md: An atom with a full outer shell, a **duplet** or an **octet**, is stable. Other atoms **lose, gain or share** electrons to get one.

headers: Easier route to a full shell

visual.alt: Table of four atoms and the easier way each reaches a full outer shell

slides.narration: Compare each atom with its nearest full shell. Sodium has one outer electron, so losing it is easy. Chlorine has seven, so gaining one is easy. Metals tend to lose electrons and non-metals tend to gain them.

slides.heading: Cations and anions
slides.body_md: An atom that **loses** electrons becomes a positive ion, a **cation**. An atom that **gains** electrons becomes a negative ion, an **anion**.

visual.alt: Table of four atoms, the electrons lost or gained, the ion formed and its configuration

slides.narration: Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is positive. Gaining electrons leaves more electrons than protons, so the ion is negative. Notice that each ion now has a full outer shell.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: potassium and fluorine ions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Show how a potassium atom (atomic number 19) and a fluorine atom (atomic number 9) form ions.

**Step 1.** Potassium: **2, 8, 8, 1**. It loses its 1 outer electron: $\ce{K -> K^+ + e-}$, ion **2, 8, 8**.

**Step 2.** Fluorine: **2, 7**. It gains 1 electron: $\ce{F + e- -> F-}$, ion **2, 8**.

visual.alt: Table showing the electron arrangement of potassium and fluorine before and after ion formation

slides.narration: Potassium has one electron in its outer fourth shell. Losing it leaves the stable arrangement two, eight, eight. Fluorine has seven outer electrons and gains one to complete its octet. So potassium makes a positive ion and fluorine a negative ion.

slides.heading: Quick check: ion charge
slides.body_md: How many electrons does oxygen need?

visual.alt: Configuration of an oxygen atom

slides.narration: An oxygen atom has the configuration two, six. What ion does it form?

slides.heading: The electrovalent bond
slides.body_md: The **electrovalent (ionic) bond** is formed by the **complete transfer** of electrons from one atom to another. The oppositely charged ions are held together by **electrostatic attraction**.

visual.alt: Flow showing atoms becoming ions that attract each other in an electrovalent bond

slides.narration: In an electrovalent bond electrons are transferred completely, not shared. The metal atom becomes a positive ion and the non-metal atom a negative ion. The strong attraction between these opposite charges is the bond.

slides.heading: Sodium chloride
slides.body_md: A sodium atom (2, 8, 1) gives **one** electron to a chlorine atom (2, 8, 7). Both ions have a full outer shell.

visual.alt: Orbit structure diagram for the formation of sodium chloride by transfer of one electron

slides.narration: Look at the orbit structure. The crosses are electrons of sodium and the dots are electrons of chlorine. Sodium gives its single outer electron to chlorine. The sodium ion has two, eight and the chloride ion has two, eight, eight. They attract each other to form sodium chloride.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: sodium oxide
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Sodium (2, 8, 1) reacts with oxygen (2, 6). Find the ions and the formula.

**Step 1.** Oxygen needs **2** electrons. Each sodium atom gives only **1**, so **2** sodium atoms are needed.

**Step 2.** Ions: 2 $\ce{Na^+}$ and 1 $\ce{O^2-}$; charges: $2 \times (+1) + (-2) = 0$.

**Step 3.** Formula **Na₂O**.

visual.alt: Table showing the atoms needed to make sodium oxide

slides.narration: Oxygen has to take two electrons, but each sodium atom can give only one. So two sodium atoms are needed for every oxygen atom. Two positive charges balance two negative charges, and the formula has two sodium for every oxygen.

visual.alt: Orbit structure diagram for the formation of magnesium chloride

slides.narration: Magnesium has two outer electrons. One goes to each of two chlorine atoms. The magnesium ion carries two positive charges, and each chloride ion carries one negative charge. The formula is magnesium chloride, with one magnesium for every two chlorine.

slides.heading: Calcium oxide
slides.body_md: A calcium atom (2, 8, 8, 2) gives **two** electrons to one oxygen atom (2, 6). The charges, 2+ and 2−, balance in the ratio **1 : 1**.

visual.alt: Orbit structure diagram for the formation of calcium oxide

slides.narration: Calcium gives both its outer electrons to oxygen. The calcium ion has two, eight, eight and carries two positive charges. The oxide ion has two, eight and carries two negative charges. One calcium ion balances one oxide ion.

slides.heading: The ratio of ions

visual.alt: Table of five electrovalent compounds with their ions and ratios

slides.narration: The total positive charge must equal the total negative charge. So sodium chloride has a one to one ratio, and magnesium chloride has one magnesium to two chloride. Count the electrons given by the metal; they are the electrons taken by the non-metal.

slides.heading: Quick check: magnesium chloride
slides.body_md: Count the electrons given and taken.

visual.alt: The number of chlorine atoms needed for one magnesium atom

slides.narration: In magnesium chloride, how many chlorine atoms receive electrons from one magnesium atom?

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Metals lose electrons to form cations; non-metals gain electrons to form anions.
An electrovalent bond is formed by transfer of electrons; the ions attract each other.
Sodium chloride: 1 electron moves. Magnesium chloride: 2 electrons move to two chlorine atoms. Calcium oxide: 2 electrons move.
The total positive charge equals the total negative charge in the formula.

visual.alt: Summary table of the ions in three electrovalent compounds

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Metals give electrons and become positive ions. Non-metals take electrons and become negative ions. The attraction between them is the electrovalent bond, and the charges must balance in the formula.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Draw the ions with brackets and write the charge outside the top right.
Show the electrons that were transferred in a different colour or symbol.
Write the configuration of both atoms and both ions.
State that the bond is formed by transfer of electrons.

rows: Showing magnesium giving 2 electrons to one chlorine atom
Each chlorine takes one: two chlorine atoms
Leaving out the charge on the ion
In an ionic bond it is transferred

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Exam tips. Use brackets and charges for ions. Mark the transferred electrons clearly. Give the electron arrangement before and after. And say that electrons are transferred, not shared.

decks.title: Chemical Bonding — Part 2: The covalent bond and radicals
goals: Explain covalent bonding as sharing of electron pairs to complete a duplet or an octet
Draw orbit structures of the prescribed molecules showing shared pairs
Explain how breaking a covalent bond forms radicals

slides.heading: Sharing and splitting
slides.body_md: Part 2 — atoms of non-metals can **share** pairs of electrons. We then see what happens when a shared pair **breaks**.

visual.alt: Flow from atoms sharing a pair to a molecule and then radicals when the bond breaks

slides.narration: Two non-metal atoms both need electrons, so neither can give any away. They solve this by sharing. Later we see what happens when the shared pair is broken.

slides.heading: The covalent bond
slides.body_md: A **covalent bond** is formed by the **sharing of a pair of electrons** between two atoms. Each atom counts the shared electrons towards its own duplet or octet.

visual.alt: Table showing how many electrons each atom needs and how many pairs it shares

slides.narration: Each atom shares as many electrons as it needs to complete its outer shell. Hydrogen needs one and shares one pair. Oxygen needs two, nitrogen three, and carbon four. The shared electrons count for both atoms.

slides.heading: Single, double and triple bonds

visual.alt: Table of single, double and triple covalent bonds with the shared pairs and an example of each

slides.narration: One shared pair makes a single bond, two shared pairs make a double bond and three make a triple bond. Hydrogen has a single bond, oxygen has a double bond, and nitrogen has a triple bond.

slides.heading: Single bonds: hydrogen, chlorine and hydrogen chloride
slides.body_md: In each molecule one pair is shared. Chlorine keeps **three lone pairs**: seven outer electrons, one shared.

slides.narration: Each oxygen atom has six outer electrons and shares two of them in two pairs, making a double bond. Each nitrogen atom has five outer electrons and shares three, making a triple bond. Both atoms end up with an octet.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the oxygen molecule
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Show how two oxygen atoms form an $\ce{O2}$ molecule.

**Step 1.** Each oxygen atom has **6** outer electrons (2, 6) and needs **2** more.

**Step 2.** Each atom contributes **2** electrons to the shared region: **2** shared pairs (4 electrons), a double bond.

**Step 3.** Each atom: 6 + 2 = **8**, an octet. Remaining electrons: 2 lone pairs on each atom.

visual.alt: Table showing the electrons round each atom in an oxygen molecule

slides.narration: Each oxygen atom has six outer electrons and needs two more. The atoms share two pairs, which is four electrons, forming a double bond. Each atom now has eight electrons round it, with two lone pairs each.

visual.alt: Orbit structures of water and ammonia molecules

slides.narration: In water, the oxygen atom shares one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms and keeps two lone pairs. In ammonia, the nitrogen atom shares one pair with each of three hydrogen atoms and keeps a single lone pair.

slides.heading: Methane and carbon tetrachloride
slides.body_md: Carbon has four outer electrons and shares **four** pairs. Methane has four hydrogen atoms and carbon tetrachloride has four chlorine atoms.

visual.alt: Orbit structures of methane and carbon tetrachloride molecules

slides.narration: Carbon shares four pairs, one with each atom around it. In methane there is no lone pair on carbon. In carbon tetrachloride each chlorine atom also keeps three lone pairs, so every atom has an octet.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting electrons in carbon tetrachloride
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the total outer electrons, shared pairs and lone pairs in one molecule of $\ce{CCl4}$.

**Step 1.** Outer electrons: carbon 4 + four chlorine atoms 4 × 7 = 28, total **32**.

**Step 2.** Four single bonds: **4** shared pairs = 8 electrons.

**Step 3.** Left over: 32 − 8 = 24 electrons = **12** lone pairs (3 on each chlorine).

visual.alt: Table of the outer electrons, shared pairs and lone pairs in a carbon tetrachloride molecule

slides.narration: Carbon contributes four outer electrons and each of the four chlorine atoms contributes seven, which gives thirty two. Eight of them are in four shared pairs. The remaining twenty four electrons form twelve lone pairs, three on each chlorine atom.

slides.heading: Quick check: lone pairs
slides.body_md: Count the outer electrons of nitrogen.

visual.alt: The lone pairs on the nitrogen atom of an ammonia molecule

slides.narration: Nitrogen has five outer electrons and shares three of them in an ammonia molecule. How many lone pairs does the nitrogen atom keep?

slides.heading: Breaking a covalent bond: radicals
slides.body_md: When a shared pair breaks so that **each atom keeps one electron**, two **radicals** form. A radical is an atom or group with an **unpaired electron**. Radicals are very reactive.

nodes.label: Bond breaks, one electron to each
Two radicals, each with an unpaired electron

visual.alt: Flow showing a shared pair splitting so that each atom keeps one electron to form two radicals

slides.narration: A covalent bond can break in such a way that each atom takes one of the two shared electrons. The pieces are called radicals. Each has one unpaired electron, and that is why radicals are so reactive.

slides.heading: Radicals from hydrogen and chlorine
slides.body_md: $\ce{H2 -> 2H.}$ and $\ce{Cl2 ->[light] 2Cl.}$ A radical is **neutral**: it has an unpaired electron but no charge.

slides.narration: When a hydrogen molecule splits, each hydrogen atom keeps one electron. When a chlorine molecule splits in light, each chlorine atom keeps one electron and has an unpaired electron among its seven. These radicals carry no charge.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: methane to radicals
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A carbon–hydrogen bond of methane breaks so that each atom keeps one electron. Name the radicals and write the equation.

**Step 1.** The shared pair is split: the hydrogen atom takes **1** electron and the carbon part takes **1**.

**Step 2.** The products are a hydrogen radical and a **methyl radical**: $\ce{CH4 -> CH3. + H.}$

**Step 3.** Check atoms: C 1 = 1; H 4 = 3 + 1.

visual.alt: Methane splits into a methyl radical and a hydrogen radical
visual.caption: One shared pair splits; each product has an unpaired electron.

slides.narration: One of the four bonds in methane breaks, and each atom keeps one electron. The carbon part with three hydrogen atoms is called a methyl radical. The other piece is a hydrogen radical. Both have an unpaired electron.

notes.title: Chemical Bonding — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The electrovalent bond and ion formation
sections.body_md:
Atoms combine to reach a stable outer shell: a **duplet** (2, as in helium) or an **octet** (8). An atom can **lose**, **gain** or **share** electrons to do so.

- A **cation** is a positive ion, formed when an atom **loses** electrons (metals, with 1 to 3 outer electrons): $\ce{Na -> Na+ + e-}$, $\ce{Mg -> Mg^2+ + 2e-}$.
- An **anion** is a negative ion, formed when an atom **gains** electrons (non-metals, with 5 to 7 outer electrons): $\ce{Cl + e- -> Cl-}$, $\ce{O + 2e- -> O^2-}$.

The **electrovalent (ionic) bond** is the bond formed by the **complete transfer** of one or more electrons from one atom (usually a metal) to another (usually a non-metal). The oppositely charged ions attract each other: the attraction is **electrostatic**. The compound formed is an electrovalent (ionic) compound.

| Atom | Configuration | Ion | Ion configuration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sodium | 2, 8, 1 | Na⁺ | 2, 8 |
| Magnesium | 2, 8, 2 | Mg²⁺ | 2, 8 |
| Calcium | 2, 8, 8, 2 | Ca²⁺ | 2, 8, 8 |
| Chlorine | 2, 8, 7 | Cl⁻ | 2, 8, 8 |
| Oxygen | 2, 6 | O²⁻ | 2, 8 |

The ions of sodium, magnesium, oxygen and fluorine have the same arrangement as neon (2, 8); those of potassium, calcium and chlorine the same as argon (2, 8, 8). The total positive charge equals the total negative charge, which fixes the formula.

key_terms.definition_md: The bond formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom to another, the resulting ions being held together by electrostatic attraction.
A cation is a positive ion formed by loss of electrons; an anion is a negative ion formed by gain of electrons.

sections.heading: 2. Orbit structures of sodium chloride, magnesium chloride and calcium oxide
sections.body_md:
In an **orbit structure** the electrons are drawn in their shells. Show electrons of one atom as dots and of the other as crosses, draw the ions in square brackets and write the charge at the top right.

**Sodium chloride, NaCl:** sodium (2, 8, 1) gives its **one** outer electron to chlorine (2, 8, 7). Na⁺ is 2, 8 and Cl⁻ is 2, 8, 8. Ratio 1 : 1.

**Magnesium chloride, MgCl₂:** magnesium (2, 8, 2) gives **one electron to each of two** chlorine atoms. Mg²⁺ is 2, 8; each Cl⁻ is 2, 8, 8. Ratio 1 : 2.

**Calcium oxide, CaO:** calcium (2, 8, 8, 2) gives **two** electrons to oxygen (2, 6). Ca²⁺ is 2, 8, 8 and O²⁻ is 2, 8. Ratio 1 : 1.

| Compound | Cation | Anion | Electrons transferred (per formula unit) |
|---|---|---|---|
| NaCl | Na⁺ | Cl⁻ | 1 |
| MgCl₂ | Mg²⁺ | two Cl⁻ | 2 (1 to each chlorine) |
| CaO | Ca²⁺ | O²⁻ | 2 |

The same method gives potassium chloride (K⁺ and Cl⁻, 1 : 1), magnesium oxide (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, 1 : 1) and sodium oxide (two Na⁺ and one O²⁻).

sections.heading: 3. The covalent bond
sections.body_md:
A **covalent bond** is the bond formed by the **sharing of one or more pairs of electrons** between two atoms (usually non-metals), so that each atom completes its duplet or octet.

- **Single bond:** one shared pair (H–H, Cl–Cl, H–Cl).
- **Double bond:** two shared pairs (O=O).
- **Triple bond:** three shared pairs (N≡N).

| Atom | Outer electrons | Needs for duplet or octet | Pairs shared |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hydrogen | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Chlorine | 7 | 1 | 1 |
| Oxygen | 6 | 2 | 2 |
| Nitrogen | 5 | 3 | 3 |
| Carbon | 4 | 4 | 4 |

Electrons shared by two atoms count for both atoms. Electrons not shared form **lone pairs**.

key_terms.definition_md: The bond formed by the sharing of a pair or pairs of electrons between two atoms.
A pair of outer-shell electrons that is not shared.

sections.heading: 4. Orbit structures of covalent molecules
sections.body_md:
In an orbit structure of a molecule the outer shells overlap and the shared pairs sit in the overlap, one dot and one cross for each pair. Count lone pairs on each atom.

| Molecule | Outer electrons in all atoms | Shared pairs | Lone pairs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hydrogen | H₂ | 2 | 1 | 0 |
| Chlorine | Cl₂ | 14 | 1 | 6 |
| Hydrogen chloride | HCl | 8 | 1 | 3 |
| Oxygen | O₂ | 12 | 2 | 4 |
| Nitrogen | N₂ | 10 | 3 | 2 |
| Water | H₂O | 8 | 2 | 2 |
| Ammonia | NH₃ | 8 | 3 | 1 |
| Carbon tetrachloride | CCl₄ | 32 | 4 | 12 |
| Methane | CH₄ | 8 | 4 | 0 |

- **Hydrogen:** a single bond; each atom has a duplet.
- **Chlorine, hydrogen chloride:** a single bond; chlorine has three lone pairs.
- **Oxygen:** a double bond; two lone pairs on each atom. **Nitrogen:** a triple bond; one lone pair on each atom.
- **Water:** two single bonds; two lone pairs on oxygen. **Ammonia:** three single bonds; one lone pair on nitrogen.
- **Methane:** four single bonds; no lone pair. **Carbon tetrachloride:** four single bonds; three lone pairs on each chlorine.

The outer-shell electron count of every atom in each molecule is the octet (the duplet for hydrogen). The shape of the molecules is not asked at this level.

key_terms.definition_md: A pair of electrons, one contributed by each atom, that forms a single covalent bond.

sections.heading: 5. Radicals from the breaking of a covalent bond
sections.body_md:
When a covalent bond breaks so that **each atom keeps one of the two shared electrons**, the pieces are **radicals** (free radicals): atoms or groups with an **unpaired electron**. A radical has **no charge** and is very **reactive**.

- Hydrogen: $\ce{H2 -> 2H.}$
- Chlorine in light: $\ce{Cl2 ->[light] 2Cl.}$
- Methane: $\ce{CH4 -> CH3. + H.}$ (a methyl radical and a hydrogen radical)

Do not confuse these radicals with the **valency radicals** of the first chapter, such as sulphate or ammonium: those are charged groups of atoms that stay together in reactions. A free radical is a neutral species with an unpaired electron. Compare with an ion, which carries a charge and has all its electrons paired (a chloride ion has 8 outer electrons, a chlorine radical has 7).

key_terms.definition_md: An atom or group of atoms with an unpaired electron, formed when a covalent bond breaks and each atom keeps one electron.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Drawing a shared pair for an electrovalent bond, or a transferred electron for a covalent bond.
- Showing both chlorine atoms taking two electrons from magnesium, or one chlorine atom taking two.
- Leaving out the lone pairs, or writing 2 shared pairs for chlorine.
- Forgetting the brackets and the charge on ions.
- Writing a charge on a radical, or on a covalent molecule.
- Mixing up radicals (unpaired electron) with the valency radicals of the first chapter.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a configuration, an ion with its charge, the number of shared pairs or a definition.
- 2 marks: two differences, or a reason with a configuration.
- 3 marks: three structures, ions or counts.
- 10-mark structured question: a lettered orbit structure with parts of 2 to 4 marks: naming parts, configurations, equations for ion formation, drawing an orbit structure and counting shared and lone pairs.

cards.front_md: Why do atoms form bonds?
cards.back_md: To reach a stable outer shell: a duplet or an octet.

cards.front_md: What is a cation?
cards.back_md: A positive ion, formed when an atom loses electrons.

cards.front_md: What is an anion?
cards.back_md: A negative ion, formed when an atom gains electrons.

cards.front_md: What is an electrovalent bond?
cards.back_md: A bond formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom to another, the ions being held by electrostatic attraction.

cards.front_md: Which atoms usually form cations and which anions?
cards.back_md: Metals form cations; non-metals form anions.

cards.front_md: Equation for the formation of Mg²⁺?
cards.back_md: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻.

cards.front_md: Equation for the formation of Cl⁻?
cards.back_md: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻.

cards.front_md: Configuration of the oxide ion?
cards.back_md: 2, 8 (oxygen 2, 6 gains 2 electrons).

cards.front_md: Sodium chloride: electrons transferred and ions formed?
cards.back_md: Sodium gives 1 electron to chlorine: Na⁺ (2, 8) and Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8).

cards.front_md: Magnesium chloride: how do the electrons move?
cards.back_md: Magnesium gives 1 electron to each of two chlorine atoms: Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻.

cards.front_md: Calcium oxide: ions and electrons transferred?
cards.back_md: Calcium gives 2 electrons to oxygen: Ca²⁺ (2, 8, 8) and O²⁻ (2, 8).

cards.front_md: How are ions drawn in an orbit structure?
cards.back_md: In square brackets with the charge at the top right.

cards.front_md: Ratio of ions in NaCl, MgCl₂ and CaO?
What is a covalent bond?
cards.back_md: A bond formed by sharing a pair or pairs of electrons between two atoms.

cards.front_md: Single, double and triple bonds: shared pairs?
cards.back_md: 1, 2 and 3 pairs (2, 4 and 6 electrons).

cards.front_md: Which molecule has a double bond? A triple bond?
cards.back_md: Oxygen, O=O; nitrogen, N≡N.

cards.front_md: What is a lone pair?
cards.back_md: A pair of outer electrons that is not shared.

cards.front_md: Pairs shared by H, Cl, O, N and C in their compounds?
Hydrogen molecule: bond and lone pairs?
cards.back_md: A single bond; no lone pair; each atom has a duplet.

cards.front_md: Chlorine molecule: bond and lone pairs?
cards.back_md: A single bond; three lone pairs on each chlorine atom.

cards.front_md: Oxygen and nitrogen molecules: lone pairs?
cards.back_md: Two on each oxygen atom; one on each nitrogen atom.

cards.front_md: Hydrogen chloride: shared and lone pairs?
cards.back_md: One shared pair; three lone pairs on chlorine.

cards.front_md: Water: shared and lone pairs?
cards.back_md: Two shared pairs; two lone pairs on oxygen.

cards.front_md: Ammonia: shared and lone pairs?
cards.back_md: Three shared pairs; one lone pair on nitrogen.

cards.front_md: Methane and carbon tetrachloride: shared pairs?
cards.back_md: Four each; carbon has no lone pair.

cards.front_md: Where are shared electrons drawn in an orbit structure?
cards.back_md: In the overlap of the two outer shells, one dot and one cross for each pair.

cards.front_md: What is a radical?
cards.back_md: An atom or group with an unpaired electron, formed when a covalent bond breaks and each atom keeps one electron.

cards.front_md: Equation for the radicals from chlorine in light?
cards.back_md: Cl₂ → 2Cl• (two chlorine radicals).

cards.front_md: Does a radical carry a charge?
cards.back_md: No: it is neutral, unlike an ion.

cards.front_md: Exam tip: electrovalent or covalent?
cards.back_md: Transfer of electrons: electrovalent. Sharing of a pair: covalent.

questions.solution_md: Two more electrons would give 2, 8, 8, so sulphur gains two, option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A sodium atom changes into a sodium ion by losing one electron.

**Reason (R):** A sodium atom has one electron in its outermost shell.

Choose the correct option.

Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Losing the lone outer electron leaves a full shell beneath, so (R) explains (A), option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? An electrovalent bond is formed by the sharing of a pair of electrons between two atoms.
questions.solution_md: False. It is formed by the transfer of electrons; sharing gives a covalent bond.

questions.stem_md: An atom that gains electrons becomes a negatively charged ion called an ___.
questions.solution_md: An **anion**.

questions.stem_md: Write the electronic configuration of the magnesium ion, Mg²⁺.
questions.solution_md: Two, eight.

questions.stem_md: Write the equation for the formation of an oxide ion from an oxygen atom.
questions.solution_md: The atom gains two electrons.

questions.stem_md: A potassium atom has atomic number 19. How many electrons are present in a potassium ion, K⁺?
questions.solution_md: The atom has 19 electrons; the ion has lost 1: 19 − 1 = 18.

questions.stem_md: How many electrons are present in an oxide ion, O²⁻, formed from an oxygen atom of atomic number 8?
questions.solution_md: The atom has 8 electrons and the ion has gained 2: 8 + 2 = 10.

questions.stem_md: Define an electrovalent bond and name one compound that contains it.

answer.model_answer_md: It is the bond formed by the **transfer of electrons** from one atom to another, the ions formed being held together by **electrostatic attraction**. An example is **magnesium oxide** (or sodium chloride).

questions.solution_md: Transfer of electrons and attraction of ions; an example.

questions.stem_md: Explain why a sodium atom forms a positive ion but a chlorine atom forms a negative ion.

answer.model_answer_md: Sodium has **one outer electron** (2, 8, 1) and loses it, leaving **more protons than electrons**. Chlorine has **seven** (2, 8, 7) and gains one to complete its octet, giving **more electrons than protons**.

questions.solution_md: Sodium loses its one outer electron; chlorine gains one electron.

questions.stem_md: State the ion formed, and the number of electrons lost or gained, by (a) a lithium atom (2, 1), (b) a fluorine atom (2, 7) and (c) an aluminium atom (2, 8, 3).

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Li⁺**; loses **1** electron.

**(b)** **F⁻**; gains **1** electron.

**(c)** **Al³⁺**; loses **3** electrons.

questions.solution_md: Li⁺ loses 1; F⁻ gains 1; Al³⁺ loses 3.

questions.solution_md: Magnesium gives 2 electrons, one to each chlorine atom, so 2 are transferred, option (b).

questions.solution_md: O²⁻ needs two Na⁺ to balance it, giving Na₂O; the others are 1 : 1, option (a).

questions.solution_md: True. Each chlorine atom needs one electron and magnesium has two to give.

questions.solution_md: The **negative** charge.

questions.stem_md: Write the formula of the compound formed by sodium and oxygen.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{Na2O}$

questions.stem_md: Name the force that holds the sodium ions and chloride ions together in sodium chloride.

answer.model_answer_md: **Electrostatic attraction** between the oppositely charged ions.

questions.solution_md: Each formula unit needs 2 electrons (one from each of two sodium atoms): 10 × 2 = 20.

questions.stem_md: Write the equations for the formation of a magnesium ion from a magnesium atom and of a chloride ion from a chlorine atom.
questions.solution_md: Mg loses two electrons; Cl gains one.

questions.stem_md: Explain why one magnesium atom combines with two chlorine atoms and not with one.

answer.model_answer_md: A magnesium atom has **two outer electrons** to give, whereas a chlorine atom can take **only one** to complete its octet. So **two chlorine atoms** are needed to take the two electrons.

questions.solution_md: Magnesium gives two; each chlorine takes one.

marking_scheme.step: Magnesium has two electrons to give
Each chlorine takes one, so two are needed

questions.stem_md: Give the electron arrangement of a calcium ion and name the noble gas atom that has the same arrangement.

answer.model_answer_md: The calcium ion, Ca²⁺, is **2, 8, 8**, the same as an **argon** atom.

questions.solution_md: 2, 8, 8; argon.

questions.stem_md: Sodium (2, 8, 1) combines with oxygen (2, 6). (a) How many sodium atoms are needed for one oxygen atom? (b) Write the ions formed with their charges. (c) Write the formula of the compound.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Two**, since oxygen takes 2 electrons and each sodium atom gives 1.

**(b)** Two **Na⁺** ions and one **O²⁻** ion.

**(c)** $\ce{Na2O}$

questions.solution_md: Two Na atoms; 2 Na⁺ and O²⁻; Na₂O.

questions.stem_md: In the formation of calcium oxide from calcium (2, 8, 8, 2) and oxygen (2, 6), state (a) how many electrons are transferred, (b) the charge on the calcium ion and on the oxide ion, (c) the arrangement of the oxide ion.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Two** electrons.

**(b)** Calcium ion **2+**; oxide ion **2−**.

**(c)** **2, 8**.

questions.solution_md: Two electrons; 2+ and 2−; 2, 8.

questions.stem_md: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms

options.text_md: attract each other as opposite ions
share one or more pairs of electrons

questions.solution_md: Sharing of electron pairs forms the covalent bond, option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which of these molecules contains a triple bond between its atoms?
questions.solution_md: Each nitrogen atom needs three electrons, so three pairs are shared, option (b).

questions.stem_md: The number of electrons shared between the two atoms in a molecule of oxygen is
questions.solution_md: A double bond has two shared pairs, 4 electrons, option (a).

questions.stem_md: An atom X has the configuration 2, 8, 6. It combines with hydrogen to form a molecule in which X shares

options.text_md: 6 pairs, and the formula is H₆X
1 pair, and the formula is HX
2 pairs, and the formula is HX₂
2 pairs, and the formula is H₂X

questions.solution_md: X needs two electrons, so it shares two pairs, one with each of two hydrogen atoms, option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which pair of atoms is most likely to be joined by a covalent bond?
questions.solution_md: Two non-metals share electrons; the other pairs are a metal with a non-metal, option (d).

questions.stem_md: When two hydrogen atoms form a hydrogen molecule, each atom attains the electron arrangement of
questions.solution_md: Sharing one pair gives each hydrogen atom two electrons, as in helium, option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Hydrogen chloride is a covalent compound.

**Reason (R):** Hydrogen chloride is a gas at room temperature.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the bond is covalent because the atoms share a pair, not because the compound is a gas, option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A double covalent bond involves four electrons shared between two atoms.
questions.solution_md: True. A double bond is two shared pairs.

questions.stem_md: A covalent bond formed by sharing three pairs of electrons is called a ___ bond.
questions.solution_md: A **triple** bond.

questions.stem_md: State the number of electrons shared in a triple covalent bond.

answer.model_answer_md: **Six** (three pairs).

questions.solution_md: Six.

questions.stem_md: How many electrons are shared between the two atoms in a nitrogen molecule?
questions.solution_md: Three pairs are shared: 3 × 2 = 6.

questions.stem_md: Define a covalent bond and name a molecule that has a double bond.

answer.model_answer_md: A covalent bond is formed by the **sharing of a pair (or pairs) of electrons** between two atoms. The **oxygen** molecule has a double bond.

questions.solution_md: Sharing of electron pairs; oxygen.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between the way an electrovalent bond and a covalent bond are formed.

answer.model_answer_md: In an **electrovalent** bond electrons are **transferred** from one atom to another, forming **ions**. In a **covalent** bond electron pairs are **shared**, forming **molecules**, and no ions are formed.

questions.solution_md: Transfer against sharing; ions against molecules.

questions.stem_md: State the type of bond (single, double or triple) and the number of shared pairs in (a) a chlorine molecule, (b) an oxygen molecule and (c) a nitrogen molecule.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Single bond; **1** pair.

**(b)** Double bond; **2** pairs.

**(c)** Triple bond; **3** pairs.

questions.solution_md: Cl₂ single, 1 pair; O₂ double, 2 pairs; N₂ triple, 3 pairs.

questions.stem_md: In an orbit structure of a water molecule, the oxygen atom has

options.text_md: 2 shared pairs and no lone pair
4 shared pairs and no lone pair

questions.solution_md: Oxygen shares 2 of its 6 outer electrons with hydrogen; the other 4 form 2 lone pairs, option (a).

questions.stem_md: The number of shared pairs of electrons in one molecule of carbon tetrachloride is
questions.solution_md: Carbon makes one single bond with each of the four chlorine atoms, 4 pairs, option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which molecule has no lone pair on its central atom?
questions.solution_md: All four outer electrons of carbon are shared in methane, while N, O and S in the others keep lone pairs, option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a molecule made of two chlorine atoms, how many outer-shell electrons in all stay unshared, apart from the one shared pair?
questions.solution_md: Two atoms have 14 outer electrons; 2 are shared, so 12 are not, option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a molecule of hydrogen chloride, the chlorine atom has how many electrons round it, counting the shared pair?
questions.solution_md: Its seven outer electrons plus the one it shares make an octet, option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the orbit structure of ammonia is correct?

options.text_md: Nitrogen shares five pairs and has no lone pair
Nitrogen shares one pair and has three lone pairs
Nitrogen shares three pairs and has one lone pair

questions.solution_md: Nitrogen (2, 5) shares one pair with each of three hydrogen atoms, leaving a lone pair, option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a water molecule the oxygen atom has two lone pairs.

**Reason (R):** An oxygen atom has four electrons in its outermost shell.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Oxygen has six outer electrons (not four), two of them shared, so four remain as two lone pairs: (A) is true and (R) is false, option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a molecule of carbon tetrachloride each chlorine atom has three lone pairs.
questions.solution_md: True. Chlorine has seven outer electrons and shares one.

questions.stem_md: A pair of outer-shell electrons that is not shared with another atom is called a ___ pair.
questions.solution_md: A **lone** pair.

questions.stem_md: Name the molecule in which one atom has three lone pairs and the other atom has none, with one shared pair between them.

answer.model_answer_md: **Hydrogen chloride.**

questions.solution_md: Hydrogen chloride.

questions.stem_md: State the number of shared pairs in a molecule of methane.
questions.solution_md: Four.

questions.stem_md: Carbon has 4 outer electrons and each chlorine atom has 7. How many outer electrons are there altogether in the atoms of one molecule of carbon tetrachloride?
How many lone pairs are there in one molecule of carbon tetrachloride?
questions.solution_md: 32 outer electrons − 8 shared electrons = 24 electrons = 12 lone pairs.

questions.stem_md: State two features of the orbit structure of a water molecule.

answer.model_answer_md: The oxygen atom shares **one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms** (two single bonds) and keeps **two lone pairs**. Each hydrogen atom has a duplet and oxygen has an octet.

questions.solution_md: Two shared pairs; two lone pairs; octet and duplet.

questions.stem_md: Using its electronic configuration, explain why carbon forms four covalent bonds in methane.

answer.model_answer_md: Carbon is **2, 4**, so it has **four outer electrons** and needs **four more** to complete an octet. It therefore shares **four pairs**, one with each hydrogen atom.

questions.solution_md: Four outer electrons; four needed; four shared pairs.

questions.stem_md: State the number of shared pairs and the number of lone pairs on the central atom in (a) a water molecule, (b) an ammonia molecule and (c) a methane molecule.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 2 shared pairs; 2 lone pairs.

**(b)** 3 shared pairs; 1 lone pair.

**(c)** 4 shared pairs; no lone pair.

questions.solution_md: H₂O 2 and 2; NH₃ 3 and 1; CH₄ 4 and 0.

questions.stem_md: For hydrogen chloride, state (a) the number of outer electrons in a hydrogen atom and in a chlorine atom, (b) the number of pairs shared, (c) the number of lone pairs on chlorine.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Hydrogen **1**; chlorine **7**.

**(b)** **1** pair.

**(c)** **3** lone pairs.

questions.solution_md: 1 and 7; one pair; three lone pairs.

questions.stem_md: Match each atom in Column A with the ion it forms in Column B.
questions.solution_md: Mg gives Mg²⁺; O gives O²⁻; Na gives Na⁺; Cl gives Cl⁻; Ca gives Ca²⁺.

questions.stem_md: Radicals are formed when a covalent bond breaks in such a way that

options.text_md: one atom keeps both shared electrons
each atom keeps one of the two shared electrons
the electrons are shared among three atoms

questions.solution_md: An even split of the shared pair leaves each atom with an unpaired electron, option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these species has an unpaired electron?
questions.solution_md: A chlorine radical has seven outer electrons, one unpaired; the other species have full shells, option (a).

questions.stem_md: On breaking one carbon–hydrogen bond of methane so that each atom keeps one electron, the products are

options.text_md: a methyl radical and a hydrogen radical
a carbon ion and four hydrogen ions
a methyl ion and a hydride ion

questions.solution_md: CH₃ and H each carry an unpaired electron, option (a).

questions.stem_md: A chlorine radical differs from a chloride ion in that the radical has

options.text_md: 7 outer electrons and a charge of 1−
8 outer electrons and a charge of 1−

questions.solution_md: The radical has one unpaired electron among seven, with no charge; the ion has a complete octet and a 1− charge, option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A radical carries a positive charge.

**Reason (R):** A radical has an unpaired electron.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A radical is neutral, so (A) is false; it does have an unpaired electron, so (R) is true, option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The two chlorine radicals formed when a chlorine molecule splits each carry a charge.
questions.solution_md: False. Each keeps one electron and has no charge.

questions.stem_md: When a covalent bond breaks and each atom keeps one electron, ___ are formed.
questions.solution_md: **Radicals**.

questions.stem_md: Write the equation for the formation of radicals when a hydrogen molecule is split.
questions.solution_md: Two hydrogen radicals.

questions.stem_md: Name the radical of formula CH₃ formed from methane by breaking one carbon–hydrogen bond.

answer.model_answer_md: **Methyl radical.**

questions.solution_md: Methyl radical.

questions.stem_md: What is a radical? State one property of radicals.

answer.model_answer_md: A radical is an **atom or group of atoms with an unpaired electron**, formed when a covalent bond breaks. Radicals are **very reactive** and neutral.

questions.solution_md: Species with an unpaired electron; very reactive.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between a chlorine radical and a chloride ion.

answer.model_answer_md: The radical has **no charge**, but the chloride ion has a **1− charge**. The radical has **seven** outer electrons, one unpaired, whereas the ion has a **complete octet**.

questions.solution_md: No charge against 1−; seven outer electrons against eight.

questions.stem_md: Write equations showing the formation of radicals from (a) a hydrogen molecule, (b) a chlorine molecule in sunlight and (c) a methane molecule (one C–H bond breaks).
questions.solution_md: H₂ gives 2H•; Cl₂ gives 2Cl•; CH₄ gives CH₃• and H•.

questions.stem_md:
The diagram shows how an electrovalent compound is formed from two atoms. Its parts are lettered A to E. The atom A has the configuration 2, 8, 1 and the atom B has the configuration 2, 8, 7.

(a) Name the particles A, B, C and D. [2]

(b) What does the electron E show about how the bond is formed? [1]

(c) Write the electron arrangement of C and of D. [2]

(d) Write the equations for the formation of C from A and of D from B. [2]

(e) Name the type of bond formed and state the force that holds the two ions together. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **A** is a **sodium atom**, **B** a **chlorine atom**, **C** a **sodium ion** and **D** a **chloride ion**.

**(b)** The electron **E** was **transferred** from the sodium atom to the chlorine atom.

**(c)** **C:** 2, 8. **D:** 2, 8, 8.

**(d)** $\ce{Na -> Na+ + e-}$

$\ce{Cl + e- -> Cl-}$

**(e)** An **electrovalent (ionic) bond**, formed by transfer of an electron; the ions are held by **electrostatic attraction** between opposite charges.

questions.solution_md: Na, Cl, Na⁺, Cl⁻; transfer; 2, 8 and 2, 8, 8; two equations; electrovalent bond and electrostatic attraction.

questions.stem_md:
A student studies the formation of calcium oxide from calcium (atomic number 20) and oxygen (atomic number 8).

(a) Draw an orbit structure diagram to show the formation of calcium oxide: draw both atoms, show the electrons transferred in a different style, and draw the two ions with their charges. [4]

(b) Write the electron arrangement of each atom and of each ion. [2]

(c) Explain why calcium loses two electrons rather than gaining six. [2]

(d) Calcium also combines with chlorine. State the formula of calcium chloride and how many chlorine atoms combine with one calcium atom. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A calcium atom **(2, 8, 8, 2)** and an oxygen atom **(2, 6)** drawn in shells; the **two outer electrons of calcium** shown as crosses moving to oxygen; then **[Ca]²⁺ (2, 8, 8)** and **[O]²⁻ (2, 8)** in brackets, the oxide ion showing 8 outer electrons, two of them crosses.

**(b)** Ca **2, 8, 8, 2**; O **2, 6**; Ca²⁺ **2, 8, 8**; O²⁻ **2, 8**.

**(c)** Losing two electrons is far easier than gaining six, and it leaves a **complete outer octet** (2, 8, 8).

**(d)** $\ce{CaCl2}$; **two** chlorine atoms, one electron to each.

questions.solution_md: Orbit structure with two electrons moving; configurations; loss of two is easier; CaCl₂ with two chlorine atoms.

marking_scheme.step: Transferred electrons in a different style
8 outer electrons on the oxide ion

questions.stem_md:
The diagram shows the orbit structure of a covalent molecule made from nitrogen (atomic number 7) and hydrogen. Its parts are lettered A to E.

(a) Name the atoms A and B and the part D. [3]

(b) What is C? How many such parts are there in the molecule? [2]

(c) Using the configuration of nitrogen, explain why nitrogen forms three bonds. [2]

(d) State the number of electrons round the nitrogen atom, counting the shared electrons, and the number round each hydrogen atom. [2]

(e) Write the formula of the molecule. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **A** is a **nitrogen atom**, **B** a **hydrogen atom** and **D** a **lone pair** of electrons on nitrogen.

**(b)** **C** is a **shared pair** (one dot and one cross); there are **3** in the molecule.

**(c)** Nitrogen is **2, 5**, with five outer electrons, so it needs **three more** to complete an octet and shares three pairs.

**(d)** Nitrogen has **8** electrons (3 shared pairs and 1 lone pair); each hydrogen has **2**.

**(e)** $\ce{NH3}$

questions.solution_md: Nitrogen, hydrogen, lone pair; shared pair, three; nitrogen needs three electrons; 8 and 2; NH₃.

marking_scheme.step: Needs three more, shares three pairs

questions.stem_md:
Chlorine (atomic number 17), oxygen (atomic number 8) and nitrogen (atomic number 7) each exist as molecules of two atoms.

(a) For one atom of each element state the number of outer electrons and the number of electrons it needs to complete an octet. [3]

(b) Give the number of shared pairs in each molecule and name the type of bond. [3]

(c) State the number of lone pairs on each atom in each molecule. [2]

(d) Draw the orbit structure of the molecule with the triple bond, showing the shared pairs and the lone pairs. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Chlorine **7** outer electrons, needs **1**; oxygen **6**, needs **2**; nitrogen **5**, needs **3**.

**(b)** Cl₂: **1** pair, single bond; O₂: **2** pairs, double bond; N₂: **3** pairs, triple bond.

**(c)** Cl: **3** lone pairs on each atom; O: **2**; N: **1**.

**(d)** Two nitrogen atoms (2, 5) with overlapping outer shells; **three shared pairs** (six electrons, three dots and three crosses) in the overlap; **one lone pair** on each atom, so each atom has an octet.

questions.solution_md: Outer electrons 7, 6, 5; pairs 1, 2, 3; lone pairs 3, 2, 1; N₂ orbit structure.

questions.stem_md:
Carbon (atomic number 6) forms the compounds methane, CH₄, and carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄.

(a) Write the electronic configuration of carbon and explain why it forms four bonds. [2]

(b) Draw the orbit structure of methane showing the shared pairs. [3]

(c) For carbon tetrachloride, find the total number of outer electrons in all the atoms, the number of shared pairs and the number of lone pairs. [3]

(d) State the number of lone pairs on the carbon atom and on each chlorine atom in carbon tetrachloride. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Carbon is **2, 4**: four outer electrons, so it needs **four more** and shares four pairs.

**(b)** A carbon atom (2, 4) at the centre with **four hydrogen atoms** around it; the outer shells overlap and each overlap holds **one shared pair** (one dot and one cross), so **four shared pairs** in all; carbon has an octet and each hydrogen a duplet.

**(c)** Outer electrons 4 + 4 × 7 = **32**; shared pairs **4**; lone pairs (32 − 8) ÷ 2 = **12**.

**(d)** Carbon has **no** lone pair; each chlorine has **3** lone pairs.

questions.solution_md: 2, 4 so four pairs; drawing of CH₄; 32, 4 and 12; none on carbon and three on each chlorine.

marking_scheme.step: Four shared pairs in the overlaps

questions.stem_md:
A flask of chlorine gas is exposed to bright sunlight. Some of the chlorine molecules split into chlorine radicals. Later a mixture of chlorine and methane is also exposed to light.

(a) Write the equation for the formation of chlorine radicals from a chlorine molecule. [2]

(b) State what happens to the shared pair when the molecule splits. [1]

(c) State two differences between a chlorine radical and a chloride ion. [3]

(d) Write the equation for the breaking of one carbon–hydrogen bond of methane to give radicals, and name the radical that contains carbon. [3]

(e) Give one reason why radicals are very reactive. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\ce{Cl2 ->[light] 2Cl.}$

**(b)** The shared pair is **split**, one electron going to **each** atom.

**(c)** The radical has **no charge**, the ion has a **1− charge**. The radical has **7 outer electrons**, one of them unpaired, whereas the ion has a **complete octet** with all electrons paired. (Either two of these differences.)

**(d)** $\ce{CH4 -> CH3. + H.}$; the **methyl radical**.

**(e)** Each radical has an **unpaired electron** and tends to pair it up by reacting.

questions.solution_md: Cl₂ gives 2Cl•; one electron to each atom; two differences; CH₄ gives CH₃• and H•; unpaired electron.

questions.stem_md: A positively charged ion formed when an atom loses electrons is called a
questions.solution_md: Loss of electrons gives a positive ion, a cation, option (d).

questions.stem_md: The number of electrons shared in one single covalent bond is
questions.solution_md: A single bond is one shared pair, which is two electrons, option (b).

questions.stem_md: Name the type of covalent bond between the two atoms in a molecule of nitrogen.

answer.model_answer_md: **Triple bond.**

questions.solution_md: Triple bond.

questions.stem_md: Radicals are usually very reactive because each one

options.text_md: has an unpaired electron that it tends to pair up

questions.solution_md: The unpaired electron makes the species eager to react, option (d).
